reconcile.connective: Defenders relocate the cruelty to the human invaders and read Hosea as predicting, not commanding — God justly judges covenant rebellion and merely permits the enemy's atrocity, the very act he condemns when done unprovoked.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells presses the double standard directly: God decrees that Samaria's pregnant women be ripped up yet condemns the same act in others, so the deed is approved and condemned at once.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Does God allow pregnant women to be ripped apart?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/ripped.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online), "Does God allow pregnant women to be ripped apart?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: Men often do that unjustly and wickedly, and shall be severely reckoned with for it, which yet God just permits them to do.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the double standard via the permission-not-endorsement distinction: the cruelty (Damascus/Ammon ripping up Gilead) is the human agents' wickedness, justly punished, even though God permits it as an instrument of judgment.

excerpts.excerpt_text: things which are often done by cruel enemies, when cities are sacked and plundered; and which Shalmaneser might be provoked unto by the perfidy of the king of Israel, and by the city of Samaria holding out a three years' siege.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Locates the ripping-up in the invader's hands (Shalmaneser), provoked by Israel's own perfidy — i.e. Hosea predicts the enemy's atrocity as just recompense, not a divine endorsement of the act, the harmonizing reading of the Hosea side.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Amos 1:3
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Treats this passage's tension directly, distinguishing God's permitting the atrocity (used as judgment) from the wickedness of the human agents who commit it and are reckoned with for it.
